headline: This October, Do Less in Your Garden—It Saves Native Bees
meta_description: Native bees need leaf litter, hollow stems, and bare soil to survive winter. By skipping fall cleanup, your garden becomes crucial habitat for thousands of ind…
summary_short: Skip the fall rake-up. Fallen leaves, uncut plant stems, and bare patches are where over 3,600 native bee species overwinter—and you barely have to lift a finger to help.
body:
Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, yet most people know only honeybees. The real crisis affects wild native bees—mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, and bumble bees—which are in steep decline. These solitary bees each build their own nests, lay eggs, and seal them shut, with offspring spending most of their life stages inside those cells until emerging the following year at the exact season their mother was active. The problem: your autumn garden cleanup is destroying their winter homes. The solution is almost absurdly simple—do less.

According to wildlife biologist Sam Droege at the USGS, you may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape right now. That leaf litter you're tempted to bag? Move it instead to flower borders, hedge bases, or a back corner. Bumble bee queens hibernate by burrowing into leaf mulch. Those hollow perennial stems you want to cut to the ground? Leave them at least a foot tall—tunnel-nesting bees like small carpenter bees and leafcutters depend on them for nesting. Cane fruits like raspberries only fruit in their second year anyway, so trimming them to a foot creates valuable nesting material without sacrificing next year's harvest. Don't compost cut stems either; any bees already nesting in them won't survive the process.

Bare patches of soil matter too. Most native bees nest underground in uncompacted earth—sandy or loamy soil in sunny spots works best. You don't need many; even a few square feet help. Skip the mulch and landscape fabric that would block them. Finally, keep some flowers blooming into fall: goldenrod and asters feed sweat bees and mining bees still foraging late in the season. Your wild garden corner isn't incomplete—it's essential habitat. That's the whole solution, really: leave the leaves, don't compost the stems, keep a corner untamed.
quick_facts: Over 3,600 native bee species live in the United States, most not honeybees
Wild bee offspring stay in nesting cells until emerging the following year
Leave perennial stems at least one foot tall to protect cavity-nesting bees
Bumble bee queens hibernate in leaf mulch or underground
Bare soil patches in sunny spots are essential underground nesting habitat
